title: A new project focuses on the viability of volunteer work in northern regions
content:
21.09.2026

  • Share on FaceBook
  • Share on LinkedIn

    • Project manager, PREPAREd | Arctic Centre, University of Lapland

    Senior Specialist, PREPAREd | Arctic Centre, University of Lapland

    The importance of volunteer action for societal preparedness and resilience is growing amid global polycrisis. Current global challenges are deeply interconnected and amplify one another, requiring new ways to approach crises and devise future pathways.

    A new international project, PREPAREd, led by the Arctic Centre at the University of Lapland, examines how volunteering contributes to resilient societies and what support is needed to maintain viable volunteer organisations in a rapidly changing operating environment.

    Volunteers and civil society organisations form a vital, but often less visible, part of society’s capacity to function. Their work can be seen, for example, in preparedness, search-and-rescue activities, environmental protection, and support for local communities on an everyday basis, as well as during times of disruption and crisis. Volunteering is also a central aspect of an inclusive society, offering individuals a sense of belonging and opportunities for agency and lifelong learning.

title: EU leaders visited Arktikum as a part of the European Arctic Summit held in Rovaniemi
content:
17.09.2026

  • Share on FaceBook
  • Share on LinkedIn

    • The European Arctic Summit was held in Rovaniemi 13-14 September 2026, where EU leaders gathered to address issues related to the Arctic region.

    The geopolitical significance of the Arctic continues to grow rapidly, and the aim of the European Arctic Summit held in Rovaniemi was to strengthen the EU’s common strategic approach to the region. Arktikum served as a meeting venue for the summit, where the EU leaders also got to visit the Arctic Opposites science exhibition by the Arctic Centre with the executive producer Nicolas Gunslay.

    In addition, EU politicians discussed with local representatives about current Arctic questions such as the impacts of climate change and the perspectives of the Sámi People’s, the EU’s only Indigenous People, to the changing state of the region. The Rector of the University of Lapland Antti Syväjärvi and the President of the Sámi Parliament of Finland Pirita Näkkäläjärvi took part in these discussions held in Arktikum. The President Näkkälärvi emphasized to European heads of state that sustainable Arctic security can’t be achieved without the people of the Arctic and vibrant Indigenous peoples.

title: Collaboration to find solutions for waste management in Arctic municipalities
content:
16.09.2026

  • Share on FaceBook
  • Share on LinkedIn

    • Postdoctoral Researcher | Arctic Centre

  • STRAWCO Project

    • Nadezhda Filimonova’s desire to use her research to bring tangible benefits to the residents of the Arctic led her to explore the challenges and solutions related to circular waste management.

    Nadezhda Filimonova’s path to a career as an Arctic researcher began to take shape early on. According to her own words, even before she was born.

    “My father worked as a polar researcher for over 40 years. Already in my early childhood, I heard fascinating stories about those distant places. The seed of my enthusiasm was probably planted back then.”

    During the early stages of her university studies in Sweden and Russia, Filimonova was more interested in the national level of Arctic politics, especially the geopolitical aspects. When attending a doctoral program in the United States, she ended up examining the Arctic region at city and regional levels.

title: New EU-funded project Beyond Arctic PASSION officially launched on 1st September, runs for four years
content:
10.09.2026

  • Share on FaceBook
  • Share on LinkedIn

    • Beyond Arctic PASSION works to build a more coordinated Arctic Observing System of Systems to address the challenges in the Arctic region.

    For decades, scientists, Indigenous Peoples, local communities and governments have worked to build a more coordinated Arctic Observing System that connects people, knowledge and technology. Yet, the Arctic continues to change faster than our ability to observe it. Observations remain fragmented across nations, observing infrastructures, data systems and knowledge systems, limiting our ability to address the complex environmental and societal challenges facing the region.

title: Tanja Joona appointed programme director of the ARCTIC programme
content:
10.09.2026

  • Share on FaceBook
  • Share on LinkedIn

    • Professor | Arctic Centre

    Professor Tanja Joona from the Arctic Centre of the University of Lapland has been appointed programme director of the ARCTIC programme under the Strategic Research Council (SRC), an independent body established within the Research Council of Finland(RCF).

    The Changing Arctic Region (ARCTIC) examines the ongoing, multi-layered changes in the Arctic region that result from climate change, geopolitical tensions and economic interests. The six-year SRC programmes, which are now getting under way, will continue until the autumn of 2032.

    The four consortia selected for the programme will study the effects of changes in the Arctic region on, for example, Arctic security and the environment, community livelihoods, natural resources and their use, as well as culture and tourism. They will also engage in close dialogue and cooperation with regional actors such as local and Indigenous communities. The consortia involve ten research fields and twelve organisations.

title: The Call for Abstracts for the 17th Arctic Ungulate Conference is now open
content:
03.09.2026

  • Share on FaceBook
  • Share on LinkedIn

    • The 17th Arctic Ungulate Conference (AUC) will take place on 10-14 May 2027 in Rovaniemi, Finland, and the organizers are now calling for abstracts.

    Every fourth year held AUC gathers together people working with Arctic ungulates and their economy, conservation and management. The theme for the 17th AUC is Arctic ungulates in modern environments, which sets a forum for discussion about the challenges Arctic ungulates face today with the increase of human pressure and climate change. How can these modern challenges be addressed with the help of research, management, local knowledge and policy?

    To answer this question, AUC brings together people from multiple disciplines: researchers, wildlife managers, reindeer herders and other pastoralists, students, and other professionals working with northern ungulates.

    Now, the organizers are calling for abstracts with a maximum of 300 words. Abstract can be either for an oral or poster presentation. Please note, that abstracts should be written only in English and in a text-only form.

    Categories:

  • Modern Challenges & Solutions I: Technological Advances and Best Practices

title: Call for Papers: 14th Volume of Current Developments in Arctic Law
content:
03.08.2026

  • CDAL_Authors_Guidelines (.pdf 154.2 KB)
  • Share on FaceBook
  • Share on LinkedIn

    • The next volume is to be published in December 2026, submission deadline is in the end of October.

    The University of the Arctic’s Thematic Network on Arctic Law, in collaboration with the Northern Institute for Environmental and Minority Law (NIEM) at the Arctic Centre of the University of Lapland, invites submissions for the 14th volume of “Current Developments in Arctic Law” (CDAL).

    The call for papers is for short academic articles, review papers, or summaries of research or projects related to Arctic law and policy.

    The publication is open access, though it is not strictly peer reviewed. Contributions should ideally be between 1000 and 3000 words; longer papers are also welcome. The volume is expected to be published in December 2026.

    Submission Guidelines:

  • Types of Contributions: Short academic articles, review papers, or summaries of research or projects.
  • Length: Ideally between 1000 and 3000 words. Longer papers are also welcome!
  • Publication: Open-access scientific publication, though not strictly peer-reviewed.
  • Deadline: October 30, 2026.
  • Expected Release: December 2026.

title: New project to examine the use of AI in shipping
content:
25.06.2026

  • Share on FaceBook
  • Share on LinkedIn

    • Research Professor | Arctic Centre

    AUTO-MARE project aims to develop framework for environmentally just, transparent, and accountable use of AI in shipping industry.

    The Critical Arctic Studies’ research team at the Arctic centre of the University of Lapland was granted funding for AUTO-MARE project – Autonomous Technologies for Ocean Governance: Maritime Autonomy, Responsibility, and Environment (2026–2029).

    Project will develop justice-centred governance models specific to Nordic and Baltic maritime domains, shaping a future where the Artificial Intelligence (AI) innovation contributes to strengthening marine life rather undermining it.

    AUTO-MARE examines the use of AI in shipping, focusing on its governance and responsible deployment. Drawing on the posthuman theory, the project analyses shipping practices as series of socio-technical relations, where the marine environment is at risk to be treated as blank data landscapes ready for optimisation. Project aims to develop framework for environmentally just, transparent, and accountable use of AI in shipping industry.

title: New funding to suport community-based green transition projects in the Arctic
content:
18.06.2026

  • Share on FaceBook
  • Share on LinkedIn

    • The project aims at supporting fair, transparent, and locally accepted green transition projects in the Arctic region. The project includes Nordic and Canadian partners.

    The Nordic Council of Ministers has granted funding through the Nordic Arctic Programme to a project that focuses on fair green transition. Project is led by the Arctic Centre at the University of Lapland and the partners are the Lapland University of Applied Sciences, Nord University (Norway), Luleå University of Technology (Sweden), and the University of Montréal (Canada).

    The project Community-based Benefit-Sharing Toolkit for Arctic Green Transition (CoBest-Arctic) develops and pilots a community-based, rights-based benefit-sharing toolkit aimed at supporting fair, transparent, and locally accepted green transition projects in the Arctic region.

title: The World’s Most Valuable Clock preserves valuable moments of life
content:
15.06.2026

  • Share on FaceBook
  • Share on LinkedIn

    • University Researcher | Arctic Centre

    The World’s Most Valuable Clock is an artwork created as part of the Oulu2026 Climate Clock Project. Arctic Centre researchers Sirpa Rasmus and Sari Stark shared their valuable knowledge and expertise as contributions to the project.

    The artistic duo behind this ingenious clockwork are Tellervo Kalleinen and Oliver Kochta-Kalleinen. The clock was created as part of the Climate Clock series of artworks. Its purpose is to showcase and preserve significant moments based on events identified by the residents of Oulu in 2025. The artwork forms part of the Oulu2026 European Capital of Culture programme.
